IRD21 · Pathology · Study Guide

Rheumatologic Diseases

Learning objectives

  1. LO 1Recognize how lupus, Sjögren syndrome and systemic sclerosis show up in real patients: who gets each one and which signs and symptoms point to it.
  2. LO 2Know which blood tests help make these diagnoses, read their results inside a case, and use repeated values to follow disease activity and steer treatment.
  3. LO 3Explain how a breakdown of self-tolerance (genes, environmental triggers, poor clearance of dead-cell debris, cytokines, hypersensitivity injury) produces these diseases.
  4. LO 4Name the main organs each disease attacks and the hallmark biopsy or tissue findings for each.
  5. LO 5Pick broad treatment approaches according to which manifestation is driving the problem.

MAPBig picture

  • Rheumatology = systemic autoimmune disease → many organs at once → ANA is the common screen
    • All three: women ≫ men · ANA-positive · overlap is common
  • SLE → nuclear antigens exposed → ANA → type II (cytopenias) + type III (nephritis, serositis) → ↓C3/C4
    • Confirm: anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith · Follow: anti-dsDNA + complement
  • Sjögren → lymphocytes invade lacrimal + salivary glands → sicca → caries, eye damage
    • Anti-SSA/SSB · focal periductal lymphocytes · ↑ B-cell lymphoma
  • Scleroderma → fibrosis (collagen) + vasculopathy (intimal thickening) → tight skin, Raynaud, organ failure
    • Scl-70 · centromere · RNA pol III → antibody predicts subtype
  • Pathology → interface dermatitis · full-house class IV GN · Libman–Sacks · sialadenitis · dermal collagen
  • Treatment → control activity (protect nephrons + arteries) · target IFN/BAFF · watch the fetus, kidneys, lungs

LO 1Clinical features of SLE, Sjögren and sclerodermaWho gets each disease and what it looks like at the bedside

By the end: you can read a vignette and name SLE, Sjögren syndrome or systemic sclerosis from the demographics and the signs, and list the features of each (including CREST and the cutaneous lupus subtypes).
Q1. What is "rheumatology," and what do the three diseases have in common?
  • Rheumatologic disease (loosely defined) = systemic autoimmune disease that can hit many organ systems at once.
  • Shared themes across SLE, Sjögren and scleroderma:
    • Autoantibodies (all are usually ANA-positive).
    • Strong female predominance.
    • Each has a signature organ pattern and a feared complication (below).

SLE Systemic lupus erythematosus

Who: women ≈ 10× men · ages 20s–40s · more common + severe in African American, Native American, Hispanic patients

Core: multisystem, autoantibody-driven (immune complexes)

Clues: malar rash · painless oral ulcers · arthritis · serositis · cytopenias · nephritis

Ab: ANA (screen) · anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith (specific) · ↓C3/C4

Feared: lupus nephritis → ESRD; accelerated CAD

SjS Sjögren syndrome

Who: women 10–20× men · primary or secondary (with another autoimmune disease)

Core: autoimmune attack on exocrine glands (lacrimal, salivary)

Clues: sicca (dry eyes + dry mouth) · dental caries · dysphagia · joint pain · parotid swelling

Ab: anti-SSA/Ro + anti-SSB/La (≈ 70%)

Feared: B-cell lymphoma (MALT, DLBCL)

SSc Scleroderma (systemic sclerosis)

Core: fibrosis of many tissues (skin almost always) + vasculopathy + autoantibodies

Clues: Raynaud (often years first) → progressive skin tightening · CREST features · digital ulcers

Ab: anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) · anti-centromere · anti-RNA pol III

Feared: ILD · pulmonary hypertension · renal crisis

CheckWhich of the three diseases is the one most defined by low blood counts?
SLE. Leukopenia, anemia and thrombocytopenia are characteristic of lupus and help separate it from other systemic autoimmune diseases.
Q2. What does a classic SLE case look like? (Case 1)

27-year-old woman, 2 months of: fatigue · low-grade fever · 5-lb weight loss · hair loss · facial rash · oral ulcers · joint pain · left chest pain on inspiration.

FindingWhat it represents
Rash over cheeks + nose, sparing nasolabial foldsMalar rash (acute cutaneous lupus)
Mild frontal hair lossLupus alopecia (non-scarring with active disease)
Pleural rub + pleuritic pain; effusion on CXRSerositis (pleuritis)
Swollen, tender elbows, wrists, small hand jointsInflammatory arthritis
↓WBC, mild anemia, ↓plateletsCytopenias (type II hypersensitivity)
↑ creatinine, blood + protein in urine, BP 150/94, leg edemaLupus nephritis (type III)
CheckIn this case, what single lab pattern would most raise your concern for long-term morbidity?
↑ creatinine + hematuria + proteinuria → lupus nephritis, the major cause of morbidity in SLE.
Q3. How do the skin forms of lupus differ?
FeatureAcute cutaneous lupusDiscoid (chronic cutaneous) lupus
LookMalar rash sparing nasolabial folds; generalized morbilliform ("measles-like") rash that on the hands spares the knucklesScarring, disfiguring plaques, mostly above the neck (scalp, face, ears)
SymptomsPhotosensitive, non-painful, mildly itchyPhotosensitive
Scarring?NoYes → permanent hair loss from follicular plugging
Link to systemic lupusVery often has / develops SLEWeak: ≈ 5% if above the neck only → ≈ 25% if above + below the neck
  • Photosensitivity: skin left uncovered under UV develops a lupus rash; sunscreen-protected skin does not. UV can trigger both skin and systemic lupus (mechanism in LO 3).
  • Oral ulcers look like canker sores but are painless / much less painful → patients often don't know they have them → always look in the mouth.
CheckA rash leaves scars and permanent bald patches on the scalp. Acute or discoid?
Discoid (chronic cutaneous) lupus. The acute malar rash does not scar.
Step 1 HY
  • Rash that spares the nasolabial folds = SLE malar rash. Dermatomyositis facial rash typically involves the folds (plus heliotrope eyelids).
  • Gottron papules sit on the knuckles (dermatomyositis); lupus hand rash sits between them.
Step 1 trap

"Painful mouth ulcers" points away from lupus. SLE ulcers are classically painless (often found by the examiner, hard palate / buccal mucosa).

Memory tool

"Discoid = Disfiguring." Discoid scars, acute doesn't. And the more widespread the discoid, the more likely it goes systemic (5% → 25%).

Q4. What happens in the serosa, blood, kidney and heart in SLE?
  • Serositis (very characteristic): lupus inflames the linings of heart and lungs more often than the organs themselves.
    • Pleuritis → pleuritic pain, rub, effusion · Pericarditis → pericardial effusion.
    • Myocarditis and pneumonitis (organ parenchyma) are less common.
  • Hematologic: leukopenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia.
    • Anemia causes: autoimmune hemolysis · anemia of chronic disease · kidney disease.
    • Low platelets → petechiae (non-blanching pinpoint spots from bleeding out of superficial capillaries).
  • Nephritis: the MAJOR cause of morbidity. ≈ 40% develop it, usually early (first ~3–5 yrs); ≈ 10% reach ESRD within 10 years (pathology in LO 4).
  • Cardiovascular:
    • Pericardial involvement = most common.
    • Libman–Sacks endocarditis = sterile valve vegetations (uncommon but serious).
    • Coronary artery disease from accelerated atherosclerosis: ≈ 2× general-population risk, ↑ with disease activity, pathogenesis unclear.
CheckWhich is more common in SLE: pericarditis or myocarditis?
Pericarditis (serositis). Lupus favors the linings over the organ itself.
Q5. What is the outlook in SLE, and who does worst?
  • Mortality ≈ 10% at 10 years; very heterogeneous; survival has improved a lot with modern therapy.
  • Causes of death: early → active disease, infection · late → cardiovascular disease, ESRD.
  • Poor prognostic factors: male sex (rarer but more severe) · African American · renal disease, hypertension, high disease activity · antiphospholipid antibodies.
CheckA 5-year-old diagnosis of SLE in a 30-year-old woman: what is her most likely eventual cause of death decades later?
Cardiovascular disease (or ESRD). Infection and active disease dominate early.
Step 1 HY
  • Common boards causes of death in SLE: renal disease, infection, CV disease.
  • Lupus hemolysis = warm (IgG) AIHA, direct Coombs ⊕.
  • Libman–Sacks: small sterile vegetations on both sides of the leaflet, usually mitral; linked to antiphospholipid syndrome. "SLE causes LSE."
Step 1 trap

Men get SLE far less often, but male sex is a poor prognostic factor. Don't confuse "less common" with "milder."

Buzzwords
"spares nasolabial folds" → malar rash, SLE"pleural rub, young woman, cytopenias" → SLE serositis"sterile vegetations, both sides of valve" → Libman–Sacks
Q6. What does Sjögren syndrome look like? (Case 2)

52-year-old woman: worsening dry eyes + mouth · foreign-body sensation despite drops · multiple dental caries · dysphagia · joint pain. Exam: very dry tongue, angular cheilitis (fungal infection at lip corners), corneal epithelial defects.

Lymphocytesinfiltrate lacrimal + salivary glands
→
↓ tears, ↓ saliva"sicca"
→
Eyecorneal defects, gritty feeling
→
Mouthcaries on atypical surfaces, cheilitis, dysphagia
  • Definition: autoimmune disease of the exocrine organs; primary (alone) or secondary (with SLE, RA, etc.).
  • Women 10–20× men. Anti-SSA/SSB in ≈ 70%.
  • Caries at the gum line / roots (atypical surfaces): saliva normally buffers acid and clears bacteria.
  • Parotid gland infiltration → bilateral parotid swelling.
  • Extraglandular: inflammatory arthritis, pulmonary, renal, neurologic disease, and lymphoma (MALT, diffuse large B-cell).
CheckWhy do these patients get cavities in unusual places?
Loss of saliva (xerostomia): no buffering of acid, no washing away of bacteria → rapid decay at the gum line and roots.
Step 1 HY
  • Boards triad: dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) + dry mouth (xerostomia) + arthritis; often RF ⊕ and ANA ⊕.
  • Secondary Sjögren is most often with rheumatoid arthritis.
  • New, persistent, unilateral parotid enlargement in Sjögren → think MALT (marginal zone) lymphoma.
Step 1 trap

Bilateral, symmetric, fluctuating parotid swelling = Sjögren itself. A firm, enlarging, one-sided mass = lymphoma until proven otherwise.

Q7. What does scleroderma look like? (Case 3, Raynaud and CREST)

45-year-old man: progressive skin tightening over 4–5 months, 2 years of Raynaud, ANA 1:1280, anti-Scl-70 ⊕ → systemic sclerosis with secondary Raynaud.

  • Raynaud phenomenon: often primary (idiopathic); sometimes secondary to scleroderma, lupus or other autoimmune disease. Often the first symptom of scleroderma, years before skin changes.
  • Nailfold (periungual) capillaries separate the two: secondary → dilated capillaries + capillary dropout; primary → normal.
  • Scleroderma = 3 defining features: fibrosis of many tissues (skin almost always) · vasculopathy · autoantibodies.
  • Skin and face: thick, waxy, tight hands (sclerodactyly) with loss of distal bone of digits · scleroderma facies (pursed lips, loss of wrinkles) · vitiligo-like depigmentation in darker skin.
  • Digital ulcers in about half of patients (vascular occlusion) → pitting scars, digital necrosis / shortening.
  • Classification: limited vs diffuse by extent of skin involvement, but the autoantibody predicts disease type better.
  • Internal organs: interstitial lung disease · pulmonary hypertension · GI dysmotility · renal crisis (major cause of death).
CRESTFeatureWhat it is
CCalcinosisCalcium deposits in subcutaneous tissue / vessels, a response to the vasculopathy; can ulcerate and get infected
RRaynaudCold-induced white → blue → red digits
EEsophageal dysmotilityGI dysmotility → dysphagia, reflux
SSclerodactylyTight, thick, waxy finger skin
TTelangiectasiasDilated small vessels (face, lips, hands); associated with pulmonary hypertension
CheckA patient has Raynaud with normal nailfold capillaries and no other findings. Primary or secondary?
Primary (idiopathic) Raynaud. Dilated loops + dropout would suggest an underlying autoimmune disease.
Step 1 HY
  • Limited SSc (CREST): skin of distal limbs ± face, anti-centromere, slower course, late pulmonary arterial hypertension.
  • Diffuse SSc: proximal limbs + trunk, early organ disease, anti-Scl-70 (ILD) or anti-RNA pol III (renal crisis).
  • Leading cause of death in SSc: lung disease (ILD + PAH).
Step 1 trap

Raynaud + ANA ⊕ + anti-Scl-70 is not "just Raynaud disease": it is systemic sclerosis with secondary Raynaud. Primary Raynaud has no autoantibodies and normal capillaries.

Memory tool

CREST = Calcinosis, Raynaud, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasias. "Centromere = CREST" (both start with C).

Buzzwords
"pursed lips, loss of wrinkles" → scleroderma facies"dilation + dropout of nailfold capillaries" → secondary Raynaud"chalky fingertip nodule" → calcinosis

ApplyLO 1 application questions

A1A 24-year-old woman has a sun-worsened facial rash, painless palatal ulcers, knee pain and petechiae on her shins. Diagnosis, and what causes the petechiae?
SLE with immune thrombocytopenia. Antibody-coated platelets are destroyed (type II) → bleeding from superficial capillaries.
A2A patient has discoid plaques on the scalp, arms and back but no systemic findings. What is her approximate risk of SLE?
≈ 25%. Discoid lesions above and below the neck carry more risk than lesions above the neck only (≈ 5%).
A3A woman with longstanding dry eyes and mouth develops a firm, enlarging right parotid mass over 3 months. Most likely diagnosis?
B-cell lymphoma (MALT/marginal zone; can be DLBCL) arising from chronic B-cell stimulation in Sjögren syndrome.
A4A man with 2 years of cold-triggered white fingers now has tight, waxy hands and a chalky fingertip nodule. Name the disease and two CREST features present.
Systemic sclerosis. Raynaud + calcinosis (+ sclerodactyly).

LO 2Laboratory tests: diagnose, interpret, monitorScreen with ANA, confirm with specific antibodies, follow anti-dsDNA and complement

By the end: you can explain how an ANA is run and reported, why a positive ANA rarely means lupus, match every autoantibody to its disease, and say which labs track an SLE flare.
Q1. How is an ANA test done and reported?
1 · Cellswith large nuclei (e.g., HEp-2) fixed on glass
→
2 · Patient serumANAs bind nuclear antigens
→
3 · Fluorescent anti-human Igbinds the autoantibodies
→
4 · Read + diluteserial dilutions until fluorescence disappears
  • Method = indirect immunofluorescence.
  • Report = positive/negative + titer + pattern, e.g., "ANA ⊕ 1:640, speckled."
    • Titer = highest dilution that still fluoresces → higher titer = more antibody.
    • Patterns: homogeneous, speckled, nucleolar, centromere, etc.
CheckWhich is the higher antibody level: ANA 1:80 or 1:1280?
1:1280. The serum could be diluted much further and still light up.
Q2. Why does a positive ANA rarely mean lupus?
  • Sensitive: everyone with lupus has a positive ANA → a negative ANA makes SLE very unlikely (rules it out).
  • Not specific: 10–20% of people are ANA ⊕ → 30–60 million Americans vs only ~250,000 with lupus → < 1 in 100 ANA-positive people has lupus.
  • Most positives = uncertain clinical significance; others = other rheumatic disease (Sjögren, SSc, drug-induced lupus, MCTD) or non-rheumatic disease (Hashimoto, Graves, autoimmune hepatitis, PBC, chronic infection).
CheckA woman with fatigue, normal exam, normal CBC and urinalysis has ANA ⊕ 1:80. Best interpretation?
Probably an ANA of uncertain significance, not SLE. Diagnosis needs compatible clinical features ± specific antibodies.
Step 1 trap

"Best screening test for SLE" = ANA (sensitive). "Most specific test" = anti-Smith (or anti-dsDNA). Swapping these is the classic mistake.

Memory tool

SnOut / SpIn: ANA is Snsitive → negative rules Out. Anti-Smith/dsDNA are Specific → positive rules In.

Q3. Which specific antibodies matter, and what does each tell you?

Master autoantibody table

TestDiseaseKey point
ANASLE (≈100%), also SSc, Sjögren, othersScreen: sensitive, not specific
Anti-dsDNASLESpecific; in ~½ of patients; levels track disease activity (esp. nephritis)
Anti-SmithSLESpecific; does not track activity
Anti-SSA (Ro), anti-SSB (La)Sjögren (≈70%), also SLECross the placenta → neonatal lupus, congenital heart block
AntiphospholipidSLE / APSBlood clots + pregnancy morbidity; poor prognostic factor
Anti-histoneDrug-induced lupuse.g., hydralazine, anti-thyroid drugs
Complement (C3, C4)SLEBoth can be low (consumption) → diagnose + monitor
Anti-Scl-70SclerodermaTarget = DNA topoisomerase I
Anti-centromereScleroderma(boards: limited / CREST)

  • Workflow: ANA = screen → anti-dsDNA + anti-Smith = confirm → anti-dsDNA + C3/C4 = monitor.
CheckWhich two SLE labs would you repeat to see if a flare is calming down?
Anti-dsDNA titer (should fall) and C3/C4 (should rise back toward normal).
Step 1 HY

Board-only antibodies to contrast (not separate diseases in this topic):

AntibodyDisease
Rheumatoid factorAutoantibody (usually IgM) against the Fc of IgG; RA (also many Sjögren patients)
Anti-CCPRA, more specific than RF
Anti-Jo-1 (also anti-SRP, anti-Mi-2)Polymyositis / dermatomyositis
Anti-U1 RNPMixed connective tissue disease

Scleroderma subtypes: centromere → limited/CREST · Scl-70 → diffuse + ILD · RNA pol III → diffuse + renal crisis.

Step 1 trap

Anti-SSA/Ro is not "Sjögren only": it is also found in SLE and in asymptomatic mothers whose babies develop heart block. A neonate with complete heart block → test mom for anti-SSA/Ro.

Buzzwords
"titer tracks flares" → anti-dsDNA"most specific for SLE" → anti-Smith"hydralazine, older man" → anti-histone"topoisomerase I" → anti-Scl-70"DVT + pregnancy loss" → antiphospholipid
Q4. What are neonatal lupus and drug-induced lupus, and how do labs reveal them?

Neonatal lupus

  • Passive transfer of maternal IgG anti-SSA/SSB across the placenta.
  • Skin rash → resolves by ~6 months (as maternal IgG clears).
  • Heart: antibodies damage the developing conduction system → permanent congenital heart block.
  • Pregnant women with SLE/Sjögren and ⊕ SSA/SSB → serial fetal echocardiograms (mid-gestation).

Drug-induced lupus

  • Anti-histone antibodies.
  • Triggers: hydralazine, anti-thyroid drugs.
  • Clue: atypical patient (e.g., older man) with arthralgia, rash, serositis.
  • Usually resolves after stopping the drug.
CheckWhy does the neonatal rash go away but the heart block stays?
The rash fades as maternal IgG is cleared (~6 months), but the conduction tissue was permanently damaged during development.
Step 1 HY
  • Other drug-induced lupus triggers boards love: procainamide, isoniazid, minocycline, TNF-α inhibitors. Kidney + CNS usually spared; anti-dsDNA usually negative.
  • Antiphospholipid: lupus anticoagulant prolongs PTT in vitro but is pro-thrombotic in vivo; can cause a false-positive VDRL.
Memory tool

"Drugs need HISTory": anti-HISTone = drug-induced. "Ro blocks the baby's heart": anti-Ro → congenital heart block.

ApplyLO 2 application questions

A1A woman with SLE on therapy has rising anti-dsDNA, falling C3 and C4, and new hematuria and proteinuria. Interpret.
Lupus flare with nephritis. More immune complexes → complement consumption; escalate therapy to protect nephrons.
A2A 60-year-old man on hydralazine has arthralgias, rash and pleuritic pain; ANA and anti-histone are positive. Next step?
Stop hydralazine. Drug-induced lupus usually resolves after withdrawal.
A3A woman with SLE has had a DVT and two second-trimester losses. Which antibody, and what does it mean for prognosis?
Antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein I) → thrombosis + pregnancy morbidity; a poor prognostic factor.
A4A 35-year-old woman with cold-induced white-then-blue fingers has dilated nailfold capillaries with areas of dropout. What next?
Treat as secondary Raynaud → check ANA and scleroderma antibodies (Scl-70, centromere, RNA pol III).

LO 3Mechanisms of autoimmunityGenes + triggers → too much self-DNA → ANA → type I IFN loop → type II and III injury

By the end: you can draw the lupus loop from UV injury to persistent ANA, name the T-cell and cytokine changes, and assign each SLE manifestation to type II or type III hypersensitivity.
Q1. What makes someone susceptible? (genes + environment)

Genetics

  • Twin studies / family clustering: monozygotic concordance > dizygotic.
  • Rare monogenic forms: early-onset, severe (e.g., C1q deficiency, other single-gene defects).
  • GWAS: HLA, STAT4, IRF5, BLK, ITGAM.
  • Usual case = many polymorphisms + environmental triggers.

Environment

  • UV light → damage → more exposed nuclear antigens + apoptotic material.
  • Estrogen: women ≈10× men; earlier menarche ↑ risk; Klinefelter (XXY) men ↑ risk.
  • Medications: hydralazine, anti-thyroid drugs.
  • Smoking, obesity, ?diet (healthy lifestyle matters).
  • Viruses: EBV; SLE patients carry more EBV-infected B cells → inflammatory transcription.
  • Microbiome: fluctuations of certain bacteria (e.g., Ruminococcus) can trigger flares.
CheckWhy is a man with Klinefelter syndrome at higher risk of SLE?
More estrogen exposure (and an extra X chromosome carrying immune genes).
Step 1 HY

Deficiency of early classical complement (C1q, C2, C4) strongly predisposes to SLE: these proteins help clear immune complexes and apoptotic debris.

Q2. How do self-DNA and type I interferon build the lupus loop?
  1. Too much apoptotic debris, too little cleanup: UV and other injury → apoptotic blebs that are not cleared → normally hidden nuclear antigens are exposed.
  2. NETosis: neutrophils keep arriving at the uncleared debris and die by releasing nuclear material as extracellular lattice (NET) structures → more self-DNA, more inflammation.
  3. Loss of tolerance: autoreactive B and T cells are not removed → autoantibody (ANA) production.
    • ↑ Tfh (drive germinal centers → antibodies) and ↑ Th17 (pro-inflammatory).
    • ↓ Treg and ↓ CD8⁺ T cells (which normally help remove autoreactive T/B cells).
  4. ANA–nuclear antigen immune complexes are taken up by B cells and dendritic cells → nucleic acids engage endosomal TLRs → type I interferon.
  5. Type I IFN + BAFF (B-cell activating factor = BLyS, B-lymphocyte stimulator: survival of autoreactive B cells) → persistent, high-level IgG ANA → loop repeats.
CheckLupus is called a disease of excess of which interferon?
Type I interferon (IFN-α/β), not interferon-gamma.
Step 1 trap

SLE's interferon signature is type I (IFN-α), made largely by plasmacytoid dendritic cells. IFN-γ (type II) is the Th1 / macrophage cytokine; don't swap them.

Memory tool

Think of lupus as a "messy house": trash (apoptotic DNA) isn't taken out → neutrophils throw more trash (NETs) → the immune system starts reacting to the trash (ANA) → the alarm (type I IFN) keeps ringing.

Q3. How do the antibodies actually damage tissue?
MechanismHowSLE manifestations
Type II hypersensitivity (antibody-mediated)Autoantibody binds antigen fixed on a cell surface → opsonization + destructionHemolytic anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia
Type III hypersensitivity (immune complex)Antigen–antibody complexes deposit in tissue (glomeruli, vessel walls) → complement activationNephritis, serositis, vasculitis, skin
  • Both activate the classical pathway → complement consumption → hypocomplementemia (↓C3, ↓C4): SLE is a "disease of hypocomplementemia."
  • Fragments: C3a, C5a → inflammation · C3b → opsonization + phagocytosis · MAC → lysis.
  • Sjögren: lymphocytes infiltrate and destroy exocrine glands; chronic B-cell stimulation → clonal expansion → lymphoma.
  • Scleroderma: autoimmunity + fibroblast activation → excess collagen, plus vascular injury (intimal thickening).
CheckAn SLE patient has a positive direct Coombs test and reticulocytosis. Which hypersensitivity type?
Type II: anti-RBC antibodies.
Step 1 HY
  • SLE is the classic disease with both type II and type III hypersensitivity.
  • Other type III classics: serum sickness, Arthus reaction, post-streptococcal GN, PAN.
Buzzwords
"NETs / NETosis" → neutrophil extracellular traps, self-DNA"BLyS / BAFF" → B-cell survival, SLE"hypocomplementemia" → active SLE

ApplyLO 3 application questions

A1A woman with SLE flares after a beach vacation. Explain the cellular sequence.
UV → keratinocyte apoptosis → uncleared nuclear antigens (+ NETosis) → more ANA immune complexes → type I IFN → flare.
A2A child with early-onset severe lupus has a single-gene defect. Which complement component is the classic culprit, and why?
C1q. It is needed to clear apoptotic debris and immune complexes.
A3Predict what happens to anti-dsDNA titers if a drug blocks the type I interferon receptor.
They should fall over time: IFN normally drives B-cell activation and persistent ANA production.

LO 4Organ systems and pathologic findingsInterface dermatitis, full-house GN, Libman–Sacks, sialadenitis, collagen and intimal thickening

By the end: you can name the hallmark biopsy finding for each disease and site, and recognize them in images.
Q1. What does lupus skin look like under the microscope?
  • Interface dermatitis = inflammation at the dermal–epidermal junction (DEJ).
  • Key feature: vacuolization of the basal layer (basal keratinocyte injury).
  • Points to cutaneous lupus (also seen in dermatomyositis); a likely Step 1 clue.
CheckWhere exactly is the damage in interface dermatitis?
At the junction between epidermis and dermis, with vacuolated basal cells.
Step 1 HY

Direct immunofluorescence of lupus skin: granular IgG/IgM/C3 band along the DEJ ("lupus band").

Step 1 trap

Linear IgG/C3 at the basement membrane with tense blisters = bullous pemphigoid, not lupus. Lupus deposits are granular with interface change.

Q2. What does the kidney show in lupus nephritis?
  • Class IV lupus nephritis = membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis pattern:
    • ↑ cells within the glomerulus.
    • Thickened basement membrane from immune-complex deposition → ↓ glomerular blood flow → nephron loss.
  • Light microscopy is not specific for lupus → immunofluorescence clinches it.
  • "Full house" = deposits of all immunoglobulin classes (IgG, IgA, IgM), both light chains and complement (C1q, C3).
  • C1q ⊕ → classical-pathway activation by immune complexes (type III).
  • Classic pairing: SLE + renal biopsy → membranoproliferative (class IV) GN with full-house IF.
CheckWhy is C1q staining especially telling?
It marks classical-pathway activation by immune complexes, typical of lupus.
Step 1 HY
  • Class IV (diffuse proliferative) = most common and most severe lupus nephritis; subendothelial deposits → "wire-loop" capillaries; nephritic picture ± nephrotic-range proteinuria.
  • Class V (membranous) → nephrotic syndrome.
Memory tool

"Full house" like poker: every card in the hand is showing: all Igs, κ + λ, C1q + C3.

Q3. What does the heart valve show?
  • Libman–Sacks endocarditis = non-infective (sterile) valvular vegetations in SLE.
Q4. What does the salivary gland show in Sjögren?
  • Focal lymphocytic sialadenitis = dense focal clusters of lymphocytes around ducts.
  • Remaining gland looks normal → focal, NOT diffuse disease.
  • Over time lymphocytic foci destroy acini → ↓ saliva.
CheckFocal or diffuse? Periductal or random?
Focal, periductal clusters of lymphocytes.
Step 1 HY

The diagnostic biopsy is a lip (minor salivary gland) biopsy. Useful when anti-SSA/SSB are negative (≈30% of patients).

Q5. What do skin and vessels show in scleroderma, and how does that explain the organ damage?
  • Skin: extensive dermal collagen deposition → thick, dense, homogeneous dermis → taut, waxy skin.
  • Vessels: intimal thickening (bland, concentric, non-inflammatory) → luminal narrowing / occlusion.
CheckOne vascular lesion explains digital ulcers, renal crisis and pulmonary hypertension. What is it?
Intimal thickening with luminal narrowing (scleroderma vasculopathy) in digital, renal and pulmonary arteries.

Disease-by-site summary

Disease / siteKey pathologic finding
SLE: skinInterface dermatitis (basal vacuolization at DEJ)
SLE: kidneyMembranoproliferative (class IV) GN + full-house IF
SLE: heart valveLibman–Sacks sterile vegetations
SLE: serosaPleuritis / pericarditis with effusions
Sjögren: salivary glandFocal lymphocytic sialadenitis (periductal clusters)
Scleroderma: skinExtensive dermal collagen deposition
Scleroderma: vesselsBland intimal thickening → occlusion

Memory tool

One word per disease: SLE = complexes (interface + glomeruli) · Sjögren = lymphocytes (periductal) · Scleroderma = collagen (skin + intima).

Buzzwords
"basal vacuolization at DEJ" → interface dermatitis"IgG, IgA, IgM, C1q, C3, κ, λ all ⊕" → lupus nephritis"periductal lymphocytic foci" → Sjögren"onion-skin / intimal thickening + renal crisis" → scleroderma kidney

ApplyLO 4 application questions

A1A woman with SLE has rising creatinine, hematuria, proteinuria and leg edema. Predict the biopsy.
Membranoproliferative (class IV) GN with full-house immunofluorescence.
A2A minor salivary gland biopsy shows diffuse, sheet-like replacement by monotonous lymphocytes. Why is this worrying in a Sjögren patient?
Sjögren is focal; diffuse monotonous infiltrate suggests lymphoma (MALT).
A3A scleroderma patient has progressive exertional dyspnea and basal crackles. Two possible lesions?
Interstitial lung disease (fibrosis) or pulmonary hypertension (intimal thickening of pulmonary arteries).

LO 5Treatment by manifestationProtect the nephrons, block the cytokines, watch the fetus, rescue the kidney

By the end: you can explain why preventing SLE flares matters, pick a general approach for each major manifestation, and name the labs used to guide therapy.
Q1. Why is preventing lupus flares so important? (the nephron curve)
  • Everyone loses nephrons slowly with age; each lupus nephritis flare causes a large, irreversible drop on top of that → each flare ↑ later dialysis risk.
  • CAD risk rises with disease activity, and active disease is an early cause of death.
  • → Goal: keep disease controlled / prevent flares, not just relieve symptoms.
  • Labs that guide therapy: anti-dsDNA (↑ with flares), C3/C4 (↓ with flares), creatinine, urinalysis (blood, protein), CBC.
CheckTwo patients have the same GFR today; one had three past nephritis flares. Who is closer to dialysis later in life?
The patient with past flares: each flare removed nephron reserve permanently.

Step 1 trap

Scleroderma renal crisis: the answer is an ACE inhibitor even if creatinine is rising. Avoid high-dose steroids in SSc: they precipitate renal crisis.

Memory tool

"Belimumab blocks BLyS" (B–B). "Anifrolumab = Anti-IFN-receptor" (A–A).

ApplyLO 5 application questions

A1A patient with diffuse scleroderma suddenly develops BP 210/120, headache and rapidly rising creatinine. Diagnosis and mechanism?
Scleroderma renal crisis: intimal thickening of renal vessels → ↓ renal flow → ↑ renin → malignant HTN + AKI. Boards treatment: ACE inhibitor.
A2A pregnant woman with Sjögren has anti-SSA/Ro antibodies. What monitoring does she need and why?
Serial fetal echocardiograms to catch congenital heart block from transplacental antibodies.
A3An SLE patient feels well but anti-dsDNA is climbing and C3/C4 are falling. Why act?
These signal rising activity / impending flare; preventing a nephritis flare preserves irreplaceable nephrons.

IMGImage ID drillName the finding and the disease, then click to check.

Skin biopsy of a photosensitive facial rash. Pattern?
Interface dermatitis (basal vacuolization at the DEJ) → cutaneous lupus.
Kidney IF, seven stains all bright. Name it.
"Full house" IF → lupus nephritis (class IV).
Lip biopsy, dry eyes + mouth. Lesion?
Focal lymphocytic sialadenitis → Sjögren syndrome.
Normal (left) vs tight skin (right). Key change?
Extensive dermal collagen deposition → scleroderma.
Chalky fingertip nodule + X-ray. Finding?
Calcinosis (the C of CREST) → systemic sclerosis.
Valve at autopsy, young woman with SLE. Lesion?
Libman–Sacks (sterile) endocarditis.

MCQPractice questionsClick an answer to see the explanation.

Score: 0 / 0

1A 26-year-old woman has a facial rash, arthralgias, BP 154/96 and leg edema. Urinalysis shows red cell casts and 2+ protein; C3 and C4 are low. A kidney biopsy shows hypercellular glomeruli with thickened capillary walls. Which immunofluorescence pattern is most likely?

B. Full-house IF = class IV lupus nephritis (membranoproliferative pattern). A: anti-GBM (Goodpasture). C: IgA nephropathy. D: pauci-immune (ANCA vasculitis). E: post-streptococcal GN (C1q not prominent; recent infection).

2A 31-year-old woman with SLE is followed every 3 months. Her rheumatologist wants a serum antibody whose level rises during flares, especially renal flares, and falls with treatment. Which test?

A. Anti-dsDNA correlates with disease activity (along with C3/C4). B: specific but does not track activity. C: screening test, not used to follow activity. D: drug-induced lupus. E: Sjögren / neonatal lupus.

3A newborn has a heart rate of 55/min; ECG shows complete heart block. An annular rash on the face appears at 3 weeks and resolves by 6 months. The mother is healthy but reports occasional dry eyes. Which maternal antibody is most likely?

D. Transplacental anti-SSA/Ro (± SSB/La) causes neonatal lupus: transient rash, permanent congenital heart block. Mothers may be asymptomatic or have Sjögren/SLE. A: limited SSc. B: SLE activity. C: thrombosis/pregnancy loss, not heart block. E: myositis.

4A 64-year-old man treated for 1 year with hydralazine develops fever, polyarthralgia and pleuritic chest pain. Creatinine and urinalysis are normal. ANA is positive. Which additional antibody is most likely positive?

E. Drug-induced lupus (hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, anti-thyroid drugs) → anti-histone; kidneys usually spared; resolves after stopping the drug. A/B: idiopathic SLE (usually negative here). C/D: scleroderma.

5A 58-year-old woman with 10 years of dry eyes, dry mouth and recurrent dental caries notices a firm, painless swelling of the left parotid that has grown steadily for 4 months. Which complication is most likely?

B. Sjögren syndrome ↑ B-cell lymphoma (MALT most often, also DLBCL); new, persistent, one-sided enlargement is the classic clue. A: painful, meal-related. C: commonest benign parotid tumor but not the Sjögren-linked answer. D: acute, febrile, usually bilateral. E: bilateral parotid swelling with hilar adenopathy.

6A 47-year-old woman has gritty eyes despite artificial tears and difficulty swallowing dry food. Anti-SSA and anti-SSB are negative. A lower-lip biopsy is performed. Which finding confirms the suspected diagnosis?

C. Focal lymphocytic sialadenitis = Sjögren hallmark; ~30% are SSA/SSB negative, so biopsy helps. A: not the pattern (and "diffuse" is wrong). B: sarcoidosis. D: bacterial sialadenitis. E: amyloidosis.

7A 41-year-old man with 6 months of rapidly progressive skin thickening of the arms, chest and face develops headache, BP 220/124 and a creatinine that rises from 0.9 to 2.6 mg/dL in a week. Smear shows schistocytes. Which drug is the most appropriate treatment?

A. Scleroderma renal crisis (intimal thickening → ↓ renal flow → renin ↑ → malignant HTN, AKI, microangiopathy) → ACE inhibitor. B: high-dose steroids precipitate renal crisis. C/E: do not address the renin drive. D: for TTP, not SRC.

8A 52-year-old woman has 8 years of cold-induced color changes of the fingers, tight skin limited to the fingers and face, small dilated vessels on the lips, and heartburn. Which antibody is most strongly associated with her subtype?

E. Limited systemic sclerosis / CREST → anti-centromere (slow course, late pulmonary arterial hypertension). A: diffuse SSc with ILD. B: diffuse SSc with renal crisis. C: MCTD. D: SLE.

9A 29-year-old woman has a scaly red rash on sun-exposed skin of the face and upper chest. Biopsy shows vacuolar change of basal keratinocytes with lymphocytes at the dermal–epidermal junction. Which term best describes this pattern?

A. Interface dermatitis (basal vacuolization at the DEJ) = cutaneous lupus (also dermatomyositis). B: eczema (intercellular edema). C: psoriasis. D: bullous pemphigoid. E: small-vessel vasculitis with neutrophil fragments.

10A 22-year-old woman with SLE has fatigue and jaundice. Hemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL, reticulocytes 9%, LDH ↑, haptoglobin ↓, and the direct antiglobulin test is positive for IgG. Which mechanism explains her anemia?

B. Warm autoimmune hemolysis = type II (antibody against a fixed cell antigen → opsonization). A: type III explains nephritis/serositis, not Coombs ⊕ hemolysis. C/D: wrong mechanisms. E: would show low reticulocytes and no hemolysis markers.

11Researchers note that patients with SLE have high serum levels of a TNF-family cytokine that promotes survival of autoreactive B cells. A monoclonal antibody against this cytokine is approved for SLE. Which drug is it?

C. Belimumab blocks BAFF/BLyS. A: anti-CD20 (depletes B cells, not a cytokine). B: blocks the type I IFN receptor (the other SLE cytokine target). D: anti-TNF-α (can even cause drug-induced lupus). E: anti-IL-6 receptor.

12A 33-year-old woman with SLE has had a left leg DVT and two second-trimester miscarriages. Which laboratory finding is most likely?

D. Antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant) prolong PTT in vitro, do not correct with mixing, yet are pro-thrombotic in vivo; a poor prognostic factor in SLE. A: vitamin K deficiency. B: DIC. C: platelet function defect (vWD). E: inherited, not linked to SLE.

13A 25-year-old woman with SLE has sharp chest pain that worsens on inspiration and improves when leaning forward. A friction rub is heard. Which is the most common cardiac manifestation of SLE?

E. Serositis (pericarditis) is the most common cardiac involvement; lupus affects linings more than the organ. A: less common. B: sterile vegetations, uncommon. C: not an SLE lesion per se. D: neonatal lupus in the offspring.
